Series::betaln¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signatures¶

Series Series::betaln(double other) const
Series Series::betaln(const Series& other) const

A Stable Beta Normalizer In Log Space¶

betaln() evaluates the logarithm of the beta-function normalizer elementwise:

betaln(a, b) = lgamma(a) + lgamma(b) - lgamma(a + b)

The receiver supplies a. The argument supplies b, either as one scalar constant or as a Series broadcast against the receiver. This is the preferred form for log-likelihoods and normalizers: forming three gamma values and then taking their quotient can overflow even when the logarithmic answer is finite. Use beta() only when the normalizer itself is needed.

Overloads, Broadcasting, And Precision¶

Call form

Right operand

Differentiable operands

a.betaln(value)

One double, applied to every element

a

a.betaln(b)

A broadcast-compatible Series

a and b

The Series overload follows ordinary trailing-axis broadcasting and returns the broadcast shape. Both operands must be on the same platform. Integer and boolean inputs promote to floating point; floating inputs retain their supported promoted precision. No input is mutated.

For positive a and b, this is the logarithm of the Euler beta integral and is symmetric in its arguments. The implementation is expressed through lgamma, so its real-valued continuation and poles follow that primitive: non-positive integer arguments can produce infinity or NaN. betaln() does not clamp parameters into a probability-distribution domain.

Reverse Mode¶

Writing psi for digamma():

d/da betaln(a,b) = psi(a) - psi(a+b)
d/db betaln(a,b) = psi(b) - psi(a+b)

The Series overload records both paths, including reductions required by broadcasting. The scalar overload treats other as a C++ constant.

Examples¶

1. Broadcast One Scalar Parameter¶

std::cout << pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}).betaln(3.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0986123, -2.4849066, -3.4011974]

Because B(1,b)=1/b, the first result is log(1/3).

2. Broadcast Two Series¶

auto a = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{1.0, 2.0}, {2, 1});
auto b = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0, 4.0});
std::cout << a.betaln(b);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-0.69314718, -1.0986123, -1.3862944],
  [-1.7917595, -2.4849066, -2.9957323]]

Shapes [2,1] and [3] broadcast to [2,3]; this is not a pairwise outer operation with special rules, but ordinary elementwise broadcasting.

3. Differentiate Both Series Operands¶

auto a = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({3.0, 5.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
b.tracks_slope_(true);
a.betaln(b).sum().reverse();
std::cout << "da=" << a.sensitivity() << "\ndb=" << b.sensitivity();

Output¶

da=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0833333, -0.88452381]
db=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.58333333, -0.63452381]

Shape-incompatible operands and mixed platforms fail before computation.
